seats: secular academic scholar of the Bible

fixes.row: People bless one another and call one another blessed (verb)
fixes.why: The note says of the man Jacob wrestled 'the text says no more of who he is'. Gen 32:30 (read in the Berean) has Jacob name the place Peniel, 'I have seen God face to face, and yet my life was spared'. The note is untrue to the text, and filing the blessing under 'people bless one another' settles who the giver is by the row's label.
fixes.fix: Replace the sentence with: 'In Gen 32:26-29 Jacob asks the man who wrestled with him to bless him and is blessed there; Jacob names the place Peniel, saying "I have seen God face to face" (32:30). The page does not say more of who he is.' Keep the verses here by hand, or lift 32:26 and 32:29 into a one-line note on the God-blessed row rather than claiming the giver is a person.

fixes.row: People bless one another and call one another blessed (verb)
fixes.why: One row of 49 holds two acts in two different words: bārak (give or wish a blessing) and 'ashar / makarizo (declare someone fortunate). The label joins them with 'and', and the note owns up only in the middle. Three of the four examples shown are the plain verb, so a reader takes the whole row as one act. Prov 31:28 is the only 'call blessed' one in four.
fixes.fix: Either split the ten 'call blessed' verses into their own small row ('They call her blessed': Prov 31:28, Luke 1:48, Mal 3:12, Song 6:9 ...) or put the 'call blessed' words first in the label and show one of them among the four examples. The ten should not be explained only in a note.

fixes.why: Mary's blessedness is cut across three rows by word-form: Luke 1:42 (Elizabeth, passive participle) and 1:48 (all generations will call me blessed) are in 'People bless one another'; 1:45 and 11:27-28 are in the NT 'Blessed is the one who' row. Luke 1:46-55 and 11:27-28 answer each other and the arc is lost.
fixes.fix: Add one sentence to the note of the NT adjective row (and to this row) naming Luke 1:42, 1:45 and 1:48 together, and 11:27-28 as the later turn: a woman's 'Blessed is the womb that bore You' and Jesus' 'Blessed rather are those who hear...'. No doctrinal remark.

fixes.row: “Blessed are the poor, those who mourn, the meek, those who hunger, the persecuted” (adjective)
fixes.why: The label lists only the low-status Beatitudes (poor, mourning, meek, hungry, persecuted). Matt 5:7-9 (the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers) do not fit it, and the list is the shape the page needs for the prosperity juxtaposition, not the text's own list. Rev 14:13 is one of Revelation's seven 'Blessed' sayings (1:3, 14:13, 16:15, 19:9, 20:6, 22:7, 22:14); here it is cut off from the other six, which sit in the NT row.
fixes.fix: Relabel in the text's own words: 'The Beatitudes (Matt 5:3-11, Luke 6:20-22), and blessed in trial and suffering (Jas 1:12, 1 Pet 3:14, 4:14)'. Move Rev 14:13 to the NT 'apart from the Beatitudes' row with the other six of Revelation, and say in that row's note that Revelation has seven such sayings (1:3, 14:13, 16:15, 19:9, 20:6, 22:7, 22:14).

fixes.row: “The LORD your God will bless you” (verb) and The goods row (noun)
fixes.why: The notes set the verbs and nouns for goods 'beside the verses that call the poor and the persecuted blessed' as one question. The Beatitudes are makarios (Hebrew 'ashre), a different word from bārak / berakah. The contrast reads Matthew as the answer to Deuteronomy 28, which is an interpretive step. The page itself says Ps 112:1-3 and 128:2-3 ('ashre) name house and bread, so the line between 'OT goods' and 'NT poor' is not clean in the text.
fixes.fix: In both notes add 'a different word (אַשְׁרֵי, μακάριος)' after 'verses that call the poor ... blessed' and add 'Ps 41:1 and Prov 14:21 also call the one who cares for the poor blessed'. Keep 'readers part, the page takes no side'.

fixes.row: God’s word to Abraham ... and the verses that speak of the nations blessed (verb)
fixes.why: These three do not carry God's word to Abraham. Isa 19:25 is 'Blessed be Egypt My people, Assyria the work of My hands'. Jer 4:2 in the Hebrew is a reflexive form (hithpael, 'bless themselves in Him'), where the Berean prints 'will be blessed by Him'. Ps 72:17 is the king's name. Placing them under Abraham reads the later promise back into earlier texts, even with the note. Ps 72:17 is also in another row.
fixes.fix: Take Isa 19:25, Jer 4:2 and Ps 72:17 out of this row. Give the three a one-line note on the row: 'The nations blessed without Abraham named: Ps 72:17, Isa 19:25, Jer 4:2.' Or leave them as a separately labelled sub-row. Also add a line: 'The Hebrew of Gen 12:3, 18:18, 28:14 is a passive form; of 22:18 and 26:4 a reflexive form; the Berean prints "will be blessed" for both.'

fixes.why: Two of the four examples shown first are NT (Acts 3:25, Gal 3:8), chosen above the Isaac and Jacob verses. A reader sees the promise first as the NT quotes it. The Genesis word to Isaac (26:3-4) and Jacob (28:14) is what the OT states on its own.
fixes.fix: Set the four lead examples to Gen 12:3, Gen 22:18, Gen 26:4, Gen 28:14. Keep Acts 3:25-26, Gal 3:8-9 and Heb 6:14 after the Genesis verses in the list.

fixes.row: The note of the Abraham row
fixes.why: The arc from Gen 12:2-3 to Gal 3:14 is split by word-form. Gen 12:2 (you will be a blessing) and Gal 3:14 (the blessing of Abraham, to the Gentiles) are noun verses in other rows, and the row note names Gal 3:8-9 but not 3:14. A reader following the promise ends at Heb 6:14 and misses the noun verse that states it.
fixes.fix: Add to the note: 'Gen 12:2 ("you will be a blessing") and Gal 3:14 ("the blessing promised to Abraham") are the noun form and are in the noun section.' Add the door 'blessing_of_abraham' to the "You will be a blessing" row if not already linked (it is).

fixes.row: The priests, Moses, Joshua, David and Solomon bless the people (verb)
fixes.why: Deut 27:12 says 'these tribes shall stand on Mount Gerizim to bless the people: Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, Benjamin'. The tribes bless, not priests. Josh 8:33 repeats it. 2 Sam 6:20 is David going home to bless his household. Ps 128:5 is a wish ('The LORD bless you from Zion'). Josh 14:13 is Joshua blessing Caleb (one man). The label names priests and leaders only.
fixes.fix: Widen the label: 'The priests, the tribes at Gerizim, Moses, Joshua, David and Solomon bless the people in the LORD’s name; and the wish "The LORD bless you from Zion"'. Alternatively move 2 Sam 6:20 and Josh 14:13 to the 'People bless one another' row.

fixes.row: God blessed ... (verb) and Every other use (verb)
fixes.why: The row note says verses stand under God blessed only where God is named, and Ps 67:6 reads 'God, our God, blesses us'. That names God, yet the verse is filed under 'Every other use' with a note that gives a different reason. This is inconsistent with the rule the hub states for Ps 112:2.
fixes.fix: Move Ps 67:6-7 to the 'God blessed' row. Remove it from the 'Every other use' note.

fixes.row: “Blessed be the LORD”, “Bless the LORD, O my soul”: people bless God (verb)
fixes.why: Mark 14:61, 'the Son of the Blessed One', is the divine title 'the Blessed One', not a person blessing God. The note already says it is a different usage. The row counts it as a person blessing God.
fixes.fix: Take Mark 14:61 out of the verses list and mention it in the note only (or in the adjective 'Every other use' row beside 1 Tim 1:11, 6:15, which are God called blessed).

fixes.why: 1 Cor 10:16 is Paul's 'we' and a noun (the cup of blessing). It is not an act of Jesus, yet the label names it as one of Jesus's blessings. The label is the text's words in an order that reads the communion practice back into Jesus's act. The verse also sits in the noun 'Every other use'.
fixes.fix: Remove 1 Cor 10:16 from this row and from the label; keep it in the noun 'Every other use' with a door to this row in its note.

fixes.row: Every other use (verb) — John 12:13, Jer 17:7 and Jer 17:7 as an example in the adjective row
fixes.why: Jer 17:7 and John 12:13 are filed in two rows each. Jer 17:7 is also the fourth example of the adjective row 'Blessed is the one who...', where it is the verb bārak, not 'ashre. The hub states 'a row never equates two different words' and then shows the verb as an example of the adjective row. Jer 17:5 ('cursed is the man') answers it, and the bārûk / 'ārûr pair is Deut 28:3-6 and 27:15-26.
fixes.fix: Replace Jer 17:7 among the four lead examples with Ps 1:1-style example (Ps 84:12 or Ps 2:12). Remove Jer 17:7 from the adjective list and mention it by note only, or move it to the verb row 'Blessing set against cursing', with a note that Jer 17:5 is the curse that precedes it.

fixes.row: Deuteronomy 28 blessings (verb row 3) / The blessing and the curse (noun row 1) / Blessing set against cursing (verb)
fixes.why: The bless-and-curse pair is the spine of the story from Gen 12:3 to Deut 28-30 and Num 22-24 and Gal 3:10-14, yet it is cut into five rows by word-form (verb or noun) and by speaker. A reader looking for the pair finds Gen 12:3 in Abraham, Deut 28 in the law row, Deut 30:19 in a noun row, Luke 6:28 in a fourth. Only notes tie them.
fixes.fix: Without merging across forms, add the same cross-line to each of the five notes: 'The pairing of blessing and curse runs through Gen 12:3, Num 22-24, Deut 11, 27-30, Prov 27:14, Jas 3:9-10 — see rows X, Y.' The noun 'blessing and the curse' row's lead examples should be Deut 11:26, 30:19, 23:5 (as now). Add 'doors' from the Deut 28 row to the noun row.

fixes.why: The label names three English words for one Hebrew word and the note says 'readers have long taken "bless" there as a softened word for "curse"'. Many scholars take it as a euphemism, where the Berean has already chosen 'curse'. The note presents it as a view of readers rather than the Berean's decision. This is accurate enough, but the row sits in the verb section 'Who blesses, and whom', where Job 1:5 reads as a person blessing God.
fixes.fix: In the note add: 'The Berean prints "curse" in these six; the Hebrew word is the one for "bless".' Keep the rest.

fixes.why: 'taken by deceit, sought with tears' is the label's own gloss on two verses (Gen 27:35 'came deceitfully'; Heb 12:17 'sought the blessing with tears'). It sums up a story the label need not retell. 'the dying man's' (Job 29:13) is a different sort of use from Isaac's and Moses'.
fixes.fix: Relabel: 'A blessing pronounced or bestowed: Isaac’s, Moses’; “your brother came deceitfully and took your blessing”; “he sought the blessing with tears”' or shorten to 'A blessing pronounced or bestowed: Isaac’s, Moses’, Job’s'.

worker_points.point: 1. Prosperity set side by side in three places with a no-side note
worker_points.why: The verses are fair and the labels are the text's words. But the three rows are set as a contrast with the Beatitudes row, a different word (makarios), and the Beatitudes label is trimmed to the low-status ones. See the fixes on the Beatitudes row and the two notes. With those the juxtaposition stays and the framing is neutral.
No side is taken in the note. The fixes: take Isa 19:25, Jer 4:2 and Ps 72:17 out as not carrying the Abraham promise, lead with Genesis examples, and name Gal 3:14 in the note.
The note is careful and says Matt 26:27 is a different verb. 1 Cor 10:16 should leave the 'Jesus blessed' row (Paul's 'we', not Jesus's act).
The Rom 9:5 note is fair, the page does not choose. Mark 14:61 is a title, not people blessing God; remove from the verses list.
Note present and no side taken. Add that Revelation has seven 'Blessed' sayings and shows them together.
Honest and kept. A one-line addition that the Berean chooses 'curse' is enough.
God blessed and I will bless you are by hand. Ps 67:6-7 names God and is outside the row. Gen 32:26-29 is filed under people, with a note that says the text says no more; Gen 32:30 says more.

worker_points.point: 8. Hard verses kept (Ps 137:8-9, Mal 3:15, Zech 11:5, Ps 10:3, Luke 23:29, Deut 29:19)
worker_points.why: Each is shown as the text has it. The note on Ps 137:8-9 is accurate.
Shown without comment beyond the text's 'deceitfully'. The label 'taken by deceit' in the noun row should be softened to the quoted words.

worker_points.point: 10. Rabbi seat: father's blessing, priests, Balaam as Torah on its own terms
worker_points.why: The three rows are in the text's own order and OT first. Heb 11:20-21 sit at the end of the list. The OT-first order is kept in all three.

missing.what: The seven 'Blessed' sayings of Revelation shown together (1:3, 14:13, 16:15, 19:9, 20:6, 22:7, 22:14); now split between two rows.

The other sense of the same Hebrew verb, 'kneel' (bārak, Gen 24:11, 2 Chr 6:13, Ps 95:6) is dropped from the hub and from the count; a reader of Ps 95:6 should see in a note that the verb is the same spelling, as a pointer. Check the About view or the word card shows the 3 verses (other_sense).

The blessing and curse of Deut 27-28 as one scene (the tribes on Gerizim and Ebal, 27:12-13, then the blessings 28:1-14 and the curses 28:15-68) is cut by form and by curse/blessing; only the blessing half is on this hub and the curse half sits elsewhere.

examples_checked: 25 of 25 rows' four examples read; 24 show their label. Exceptions: the adjective row 'Blessed is the one who...' shows Jer 17:7, which is the verb bārak and not the row's word ('ashre); the 'People bless one another' row shows three plain-verb examples and one 'call blessed' (Prov 31:28) and the row label joins both. Misfits found among the other verses: Isa 19:25, Jer 4:2, Ps 72:17, Deut 27:12, Josh 8:33, 2 Sam 6:20, Ps 128:5, Mark 14:61, 1 Cor 10:16, Ps 67:6-7.
summary: The hub is true to the text and takes no side on its contested points; the labels are mostly the text's own words and the notes are careful. It needs fixes where later readings enter earlier texts (Isa 19:25, Jer 4:2 and Ps 72:17 under Abraham; NT examples leading the Abraham row), where two different words share a row (the 'call blessed' verses; Jer 17:7 as an adjective example), and where the story's own arc is cut apart (Revelation's seven, Mary's blessedness, Deut 27-28 blessing and curse).
